title: Chinese AI Stocks Are Slumping, Too
gist: China's AI equity bubble has been deflating for months (STAR 50 down 40%+ since July), which Palmer reads as a broad retail-confidence downturn rather than an AI-specific shock; the damage is cushioned because equities are a small share of household wealth and AI firms lean on opaque state funding. The brief also flags weak consumer sentiment ahead of Double 11, CPEC funding and security doubts, and Nvidia/Jensen Huang influence concerns.

insights.claim: China's STAR 50 index of science and technology companies has fallen more than 40 percent since July 2026, leaving it nearly 200 points below its level at the start of the year.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Chinese tech/AI equities already went through a correction that U.S. AI stocks are only now beginning; a possible leading signal for AI valuation resets.

insights.claim: Chinese tech stocks rose significantly until summer 2026 and then fell further than the broader Shanghai exchange, which drifted down over the year.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Tech beta to the downside exceeded the market, showing the AI premium unwound faster than the broader index.

insights.so_what: If frontier capability gaps are widening while benchmarks don't show it, Chinese AI valuations premised on fast catch-up may be mispriced.

insights.so_what: The compute constraint (export controls) is binding on Chinese AI service delivery; watch for capacity rationing and chip import demand.

themes.theme: Why the correction hurts China less

insights.claim: The stock market accounts for only 5 to 6 percent of Chinese household investments, so equity declines have a smaller wealth effect than in the United States.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Chinese equity drawdowns transmit weakly to consumption compared with the U.S., where AI stock losses hit household wealth harder.
insights.quote: accounting for just 5 percent-6 percent of household investments
insights.locator: The stock market is much less central

insights.claim: Chinese AI firms rely less on private investment than U.S. peers, with their real backing likely coming from opaque government funding, especially since DeepSeek's takeoff in early 2025.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Chinese AI development is insulated from equity-market sentiment; capex is unlikely to collapse with share prices.

insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Policy support may favor AI firms that deliver broad economic and employment value over pure frontier plays.

themes.theme: CPEC and Belt and Road strain

insights.claim: Only about half of the funding promised for the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor has materialized, and Beijing declined to pay for a major railway upgrade, leaving the Asian Development Bank to step in.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: China is pulling back from BRI's flagship; multilateral and U.S.-aligned lenders are filling gaps in Pakistan.
insights.quote: Only about half the promised funding for CPEC has ever materialized
insights.locator: Only about half the promised funding

insights.claim: Intensifying Baloch separatist attacks along CPEC and rising threats to Chinese nationals are making Chinese firms reluctant to send staff to Pakistan, and some ransom kidnappings have reportedly gone unreported after companies paid.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Security risk is a hidden cost for China-linked projects in Pakistan; expect slower execution.
insights.locator: Threats to Chinese nationals in Pakistan

insights.claim: China's space plans now officially include a crewed moon landing before 2030, but Palmer does not expect it to reignite a space race; the real 'Sputnik moment' would be a Chinese achievement the U.S. hasn't matched, such as a crewed Mars mission in the 2030s.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A Chinese crewed Mars program is the event that could trigger new U.S. space spending.
insights.quote: The real Sputnik moment will come when China manages something that the United States hasn’t achieved
insights.locator: The real Sputnik moment

insights.claim: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang persuaded Trump to allow some advanced chip exports to China in return for the White House receiving a 25 percent cut, despite China hawks' concerns that Nvidia's interests diverge from U.S. interests.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Nvidia's China revenue depends on Huang's political access; a shift in Washington could tighten chip exports.
